Four
FAWR
n., adj.
Old English feower; Latin quattuor (source of “quarter,” “quaternion”); Greek tessares; Hebrew arba’ — all from Proto-Indo-European *kwetwer-. Four marks terrestrial completeness: four directions, four winds, four seasons.

Biblical Definition

Scripture employs four as the signature number of the created earth in its fullness. From the garden of Eden, where a single river parted into four riverheads (Gen 2:10), to the final apocalypse, where four angels stand at the four corners of the earth holding back the four winds (Rev 7:1), the number announces the spatial and cosmic wholeness of God’s creation. Ezekiel’s inaugural vision disclosed four living creatures, each bearing four faces and four wings (Ezek 1:5–10) — the full order of animate life gathered before the divine throne. In Revelation those same four living creatures encircle the throne (Rev 4:6–8), crying “Holy, holy, holy” without ceasing. Zechariah saw four spirits of heaven dispatched to patrol the four quarters of the earth (Zech 6:5). The four horsemen of Revelation 6 traverse the whole earth with war, famine, pestilence, and death — the totality of creaturely suffering under God’s sovereign permission. Four Gospels proclaim one Lord from four vantage points to the four corners of the inhabited world. Four great world empires rise and fall before the Ancient of Days in Daniel 7. Four rivers, four faces, four winds, four Gospels: Scripture employs the fourfold pattern wherever it would say the whole earth — the complete created order laid open before the enthroned Creator who made it, owns it, and shall renew it.

Webster 1828 Definition

The cardinal number four; in Scripture, the characteristic number of the created earth in its completeness — four directions, four winds, four living creatures — marking the totality of the creaturely order under God’s sovereign rule.

expand to see more

FOUR, adj. & n. One more than three; in the biblical pattern, the mark of terrestrial completeness. As three reaches toward the divine Trinity, four reaches outward to encompass the whole of creation in its spatial fullness: four corners of the earth, four winds, four rivers of Eden, four living creatures of the vision.

Webster (1828) observed that four is the first composite number above the Trinity. Scripture’s consistent use confirms that observation theologically: wherever the sacred text would speak of the earth in its total extent, it reaches for the number four.

Key Scripture

Genesis 2:10 — "And a river went out of Eden to water the garden; and from thence it was parted, and became into four heads."

Ezekiel 1:5 — "Also out of the midst thereof came the likeness of four living creatures. And this was their appearance; they had the likeness of a man."

Revelation 7:1 — "And after these things I saw four angels standing on the four corners of the earth, holding the four winds of the earth, that the wind should not blow on the earth, nor on the sea, nor on any tree."

Zechariah 6:5 — "And the angel answered and said unto me, These are the four spirits of the heavens, which go forth from standing before the Lord of all the earth."

Modern Corruption

Modern numerology mystifies four as a “stability number” in Pythagorean or New Age systems, severing the pattern from the God who placed it; over-schematized prophecy decoding turns fourfold imagery into calculation rather than a summons to worship.

expand to see more

New Age and Pythagorean numerology treat four as a cosmic constant of “stability” and “structure” to be harnessed — a power in the number itself. The sign is severed from the Giver, and created order points to itself rather than to its Maker. This is numerological idolatry dressed in the language of ancient wisdom.

Within popular prophecy culture, obsessive mapping of the four horsemen, four winds, and four living creatures onto contemporary geopolitical events turns apocalyptic imagery into a system of code-breaking rather than the Scripture’s own intent: to summon the church to patient endurance and worship before the Sovereign Lord of all history.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

All Indo-European languages converge on a common ancestor for four, testifying to the primacy of the number in ordering creation; the Hebrew and Greek biblical uses reflect this universal creaturely signature.

expand to see more

Old English feower — four; ancestor of modern English “four” and “fortnight.”

Latin quattuor — four; source of “quarter,” “quaternion,” “quadrant.”

Greek tessares — four; New Testament usage (Rev 4:6; 7:1); root of “tetrahedron.”

Hebrew arba’ — four; the fourth day (Gen 1:14–19) completes the luminaries framework of creation.

Proto-Indo-European *kwetwer- — the common ancestor behind all these forms, attesting four as primally human counting.

Usage

"The four winds held by four angels signify that God restrains every direction of creaturely catastrophe until His seal is set on His servants."

"Four Gospels, four vantage points, one Lord: the fourfold witness is not redundancy but the fullness of apostolic testimony reaching to the four corners of the earth."

"Ezekiel’s four living creatures with four faces showed that every order of creaturely life — man, lion, ox, eagle — exists to give glory to the enthroned God."
